hook.text: Two hunters can catch a stag together or chase rabbits alone. Together pays more, but alone is safer.

buildup.text: The stag hunt shows why cooperation is risky: it requires trusting the other person to do their part.

discovery.text: Unlike the prisoner's dilemma, both players prefer cooperation. The problem isn't incentives—it's trust.

twist.text: One bad experience makes everyone hunt rabbits. Trust is easy to lose and painfully slow to rebuild.

climax.text: The stag hunt models real life: startups need cofounders, nations need allies, teams need commitment.

punchline.text: Cooperation pays, but only if both show up.

quiz.question: What makes the stag hunt different from the prisoner's dilemma?

hook.text: A neighborhood wants a park. Everyone benefits, but nobody wants to pay. The park never gets built.

buildup.text: Free riders enjoy benefits created by others without contributing. Why pay if you get it for free?

discovery.text: Mancur Olson proved large groups suffer more: each person's share is tiny, so nobody feels responsible.

twist.text: Small groups cooperate better because each person matters more and social pressure is stronger.

climax.text: Taxes, unions, and homeowner fees exist because voluntary cooperation fails in large groups.

punchline.text: If everyone waits for someone else, nobody acts.

quiz.question: Why do large groups suffer more from free riding?

hook.text: Every fisherman knows overfishing kills the lake. Every fisherman fishes more anyway. The lake dies.

buildup.text: Collective action problems occur when individual rationality leads to group disaster.

discovery.text: Elinor Ostrom studied communities that solved this without government: shared rules, mutual monitoring.

twist.text: Ostrom found eight design principles: clear boundaries, local rules, conflict resolution, and graduated sanctions.

climax.text: She won the 2009 Nobel Prize proving that communities can self-govern common resources effectively.

punchline.text: Groups can solve what individuals can't.

quiz.question: What did Elinor Ostrom prove about collective action?

hook.text: Medieval farmers shared grazing land. Each added one more cow. Eventually the pasture was destroyed.

buildup.text: Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay argued shared resources inevitably collapse when users act selfishly.

discovery.text: The logic feels airtight: my extra cow gains me a full cow but costs everyone just a fraction of pasture.

twist.text: But Hardin was wrong about 'inevitably.' Many commons lasted centuries with community-designed rules.

climax.text: Climate change is the ultimate commons problem: the atmosphere belongs to everyone and no one.

punchline.text: Shared resources need shared rules.

quiz.question: What is the tragedy of the commons?
options: Shared resources get overused by selfish individuals

hook.text: Two friends lose each other at a festival. No phones. Where do they go to meet? Both must guess the same spot.

buildup.text: Coordination games have multiple equilibria. The challenge isn't incentives—it's picking the same option.

discovery.text: Thomas Schelling found people use 'focal points'—obvious choices that stand out. Most pick noon at the clock.

twist.text: Focal points are cultural. Americans meet at Grand Central; the Japanese pick Hachiko. Context creates consensus.

climax.text: Driving on the left or right is a coordination game: the side doesn't matter, but everyone must agree.

punchline.text: Sometimes the only problem is picking.

quiz.question: What is a focal point in coordination games?
options: An obvious choice that people gravitate toward

hook.text: You're given $10. You can send any amount to a stranger. It triples. They decide how much to return.

buildup.text: Rational self-interest says: send nothing, because the stranger should keep everything. Most people send.

discovery.text: Experiments show people send about half, and recipients return enough to reward trust. Humans aren't selfish.

twist.text: Oxytocin levels predict trust: people given synthetic oxytocin send 17% more money to strangers.

climax.text: Paul Zak's research showed trust is partly biological—our brains are wired for social bonding, not just greed.

punchline.text: Trust is the currency of cooperation.

quiz.question: What do trust game experiments reveal?
options: Most people show and reciprocate trust

hook.text: In 1980, Robert Axelrod invited game theorists to submit strategies for a repeated prisoner's dilemma tournament.

buildup.text: Complex strategies filled with tricks and prediction entered. The winner was the simplest: tit for tat.

discovery.text: Tit for tat: start by cooperating, then copy what the other player did last round. Just four lines of code.

twist.text: It won because it's nice (cooperates first), retaliatory (punishes defection), and forgiving (cooperates again).

climax.text: Tit for tat shows trust-building doesn't need intelligence. Simple reciprocity beats complex scheming.

punchline.text: Start kind, then mirror what you get.

quiz.question: Why did tit for tat win Axelrod's tournament?
options: It combined niceness, retaliation, and forgiveness

hook.text: Tit for tat has a flaw: one accidental defection triggers endless retaliation between two tit-for-tat players.

buildup.text: In a noisy world with misunderstandings, strict reciprocity spirals into mutual punishment.

discovery.text: Generous tit for tat fixes this: occasionally forgive a defection instead of punishing. Break the cycle.

twist.text: The optimal forgiveness rate is about 10%. Too forgiving invites exploitation. Too harsh invites spirals.

climax.text: In later Axelrod tournaments with noise, generous tit for tat outperformed the original. Forgiveness pays.

punchline.text: Occasionally letting it slide beats keeping score.

quiz.question: Why does generous tit for tat outperform strict tit for tat?
options: It breaks retaliation spirals caused by mistakes

hook.text: Soldiers in WWI trenches stopped shooting at mealtimes. They'd face the same enemy tomorrow, so cooperation emerged.

buildup.text: The 'shadow of the future' is how much you value tomorrow's relationship. Longer shadows mean more cooperation.

discovery.text: If a game repeats indefinitely, cooperation becomes rational: today's betrayal costs tomorrow's partnership.

twist.text: But announce the game ends in round 10 and cooperation unravels. Round 10 has no future, so defect then.

climax.text: This backward induction collapses: round 9 becomes the last real round, then 8, then 7. Trust dissolves.

punchline.text: Cooperation needs a tomorrow.

quiz.question: What does the 'shadow of the future' mean?
options: How much future interactions matter to present decisions

hook.text: A restaurant on a highway serves bad food. A restaurant in your town can't afford to. The difference is reputation.

buildup.text: Reputation turns one-shot games into repeated games: others watch your past and predict your future behavior.

discovery.text: Even a small chance that you're cooperative changes the game: rational players cooperate to maintain reputation.

twist.text: Final moves are dangerous: retiring CEOs, lame-duck presidents, and last-day employees lose reputation incentives.

climax.text: Online review systems harness reputation to enable trust between strangers. Uber, eBay, Airbnb all depend on it.

punchline.text: Your record speaks before you do.

quiz.question: Why do reputation effects promote cooperation?
options: Past behavior predicts future treatment from others

hook.text: A vampire bat returns to the roost hungry. Another bat regurgitates blood to feed it. Tomorrow, roles may reverse.

buildup.text: Direct reciprocity is 'I help you, you help me.' It requires repeated interactions between the same pair.

discovery.text: Robert Trivers showed this evolves when the cost of helping is low and the benefit to the recipient is high.

twist.text: Vampire bats actually track debts: they refuse to feed bats that didn't share before. Cheaters get cut off.

climax.text: Direct reciprocity explains grooming in primates, food sharing in humans, and alliance-building across species.

punchline.text: Help now, get helped later.

quiz.question: What condition makes direct reciprocity evolve?
options: Low cost to giver, high benefit to receiver

hook.text: You help a stranger. A different stranger helps you later. How? They heard you were a helpful person.

buildup.text: Indirect reciprocity works through reputation: help others and third parties reward you. Gossip fuels it.

discovery.text: Martin Nowak's models show indirect reciprocity works when people know each other's reputation scores.

twist.text: This explains human obsession with gossip: tracking who's trustworthy is essential for indirect reciprocity.

climax.text: Online rating systems are indirect reciprocity at scale: you review a seller, and future buyers benefit.

punchline.text: Be good, and word gets around.

quiz.question: What drives indirect reciprocity?

hook.text: In experiments, people pay their own money to punish cheaters—even when they'll never see them again.

buildup.text: Strong reciprocity means rewarding cooperators and punishing defectors even at personal cost. It's not rational.

discovery.text: Ernst Fehr showed this behavior is widespread: about 60% of people punish unfairness even in one-shot games.

twist.text: Punishment is contagious. When defectors see others get punished, cooperation rates jump to near 100%.

climax.text: Strong reciprocity may explain large-scale human cooperation: a few punishers keep everyone else honest.

punchline.text: Some people enforce fairness on principle.

quiz.question: What is strong reciprocity?
options: Punishing cheaters even at personal cost

hook.text: In the Pacific Islands, chiefs gave away everything they had. The more you gave, the more power you gained.

buildup.text: Gift economies run on generalized reciprocity: give freely, and the community returns the favor over time.

discovery.text: Marcel Mauss showed gifts create obligations. Receiving without returning destroys your social standing.

twist.text: Open-source software is a modern gift economy: developers give code freely and gain status and job offers.

climax.text: Wikipedia, Linux, and Stack Overflow all run on gift economy logic: contribute freely, gain reputation.

punchline.text: Giving freely can be the best investment.

quiz.question: How do gift economies create cooperation?
options: Via gifts that create social obligations

hook.text: Someone cuts in line. You could stay quiet—it barely costs you time. But you speak up anyway. Why?

buildup.text: Altruistic punishment means paying a cost to punish someone who violated a social norm, even without direct benefit.

discovery.text: Brain scans reveal the striatum lights up during punishment: enforcing fairness feels rewarding. It's satisfying.

twist.text: Cross-cultural studies show punishment norms vary wildly: some societies punish cooperators for making others look bad.

climax.text: Without altruistic punishers, cooperation collapses in experiments. They're the immune system of social groups.

punchline.text: Someone has to call out the cheaters.

quiz.question: Why is altruistic punishment important for cooperation?
options: It deters free riding and upholds norms

hook.text: A handshake deal works with your neighbor. A $50 million deal needs lawyers. Scale demands formal trust.

buildup.text: Contracts transform trust problems into enforcement problems. You don't need to trust; courts will enforce.

discovery.text: Oliver Williamson showed firms exist because contracts can't cover everything—some trust must be internalized.

twist.text: But most contracts never go to court. The threat of enforcement is enough. The shadow of law creates trust.

climax.text: Countries with strong contract enforcement grow faster: businesses invest more when they trust the system.

punchline.text: Good fences make good business partners.

quiz.question: Why do most contracts never go to court?
options: The threat of enforcement is enough

hook.text: Cortés burned his ships in Mexico. His soldiers couldn't retreat. The only option was to fight and win.

buildup.text: A commitment device makes defection impossible or very costly. It's voluntary self-binding to build credibility.

discovery.text: Thomas Schelling showed that limiting your own options can be strategically powerful. Weakness becomes strength.

twist.text: Wedding rings, deposit forfeits, and public promises all work the same way: raising the cost of backing out.

climax.text: NATO's nuclear strategy used commitment: station troops as 'tripwires' so any attack guarantees escalation.

punchline.text: Burn the ships to prove you'll stay.

quiz.question: What is a commitment device?
options: A way to make promise-breaking costly

hook.text: A dollar bill is just paper. It works because everyone trusts that everyone else will accept it as payment.

buildup.text: Money solves a coordination problem: without it, a baker who wants shoes must find a cobbler who wants bread.

discovery.text: This 'double coincidence of wants' problem vanishes when everyone accepts a common token. Money is trust made portable.

twist.text: Hyperinflation destroys this trust. In 2008 Zimbabwe, people used eggs as currency because dollars were worthless.

climax.text: Bitcoin tried to replace institutional trust with math. Its volatility showed trust can't be fully automated.

punchline.text: Money works because we all agree it does.

quiz.question: What problem does money solve?

hook.text: In Japan, nobody jaywalks even on empty streets. No cops, no fine. Just a norm so strong nobody breaks it.

buildup.text: Social norms are unwritten rules enforced by approval, gossip, and shame. They're cheaper than laws.

discovery.text: Cristina Bicchieri showed norms have two parts: people believe others follow the rule and believe others expect them to.

twist.text: Norms can flip fast. Smoking went from glamorous to shameful in one generation once the social expectation shifted.

climax.text: Development agencies now use norm-shifting instead of laws to fight child marriage, corruption, and littering.

punchline.text: The strongest rules are the ones nobody wrote.

quiz.question: What makes social norms powerful?
options: Beliefs about what others do and expect

hook.text: Why would you plant a tree if someone can take the fruit? Property rights make long-term investment rational.

buildup.text: Without clear ownership, people grab resources now instead of investing for later. Cooperation collapses.

discovery.text: Hernando de Soto showed that billions of dollars in assets sit 'dead' because the poor lack formal property titles.

twist.text: Property rights aren't just about things. Patents, copyrights, and spectrum rights create trust in ideas too.

climax.text: Countries with strong property rights attract more investment. Secure ownership is the foundation of markets.

punchline.text: Own it clearly, invest in it boldly.

quiz.question: Why do property rights encourage cooperation?
options: They allow long-term investment by securing ownership

hook.text: You stay in a stranger's apartment and ride in a stranger's car. Ten years ago that sounded insane. Trust changed.

buildup.text: Online reputation systems let strangers trust each other by aggregating past behavior into visible scores.

discovery.text: eBay's feedback system was revolutionary: sellers with 99%+ ratings charge 8% more than those with 97%.

twist.text: But ratings inflate. Almost everyone is 4.7+ on Airbnb. When everyone's great, the signal becomes useless.

climax.text: Platforms now use verified reviews, machine learning fraud detection, and identity verification to restore signal.

punchline.text: Stars replaced handshakes in the trust economy.

quiz.question: What problem do inflated ratings cause?

hook.text: Bitcoin's slogan: 'Don't trust—verify.' The whole point was removing the need to trust any institution.

buildup.text: Blockchain creates consensus without a central authority. No bank, no government—just math and incentives.

discovery.text: Smart contracts auto-execute when conditions are met. The code itself becomes the trusted intermediary.

twist.text: But 'trustless' just shifts trust: to code, to miners, to wallet security. The FTX collapse showed trust still matters.

climax.text: Every 'trustless' system embeds trust somewhere. The question is where, in whom, and whether users know it.

punchline.text: You can't escape trust—only relocate it.

quiz.question: Why is 'trustless' misleading for blockchain?
options: Trust shifts to code, miners, and platforms

hook.text: Uber holds your payment until the ride ends. Airbnb holds funds until check-in. Escrow builds trust by default.

buildup.text: Platform designers use game theory to structure interactions so trust emerges even between strangers.

discovery.text: Key tools: escrow, mutual ratings, identity verification, insurance, and dispute resolution create trust layers.

twist.text: The best platforms make trust invisible. You don't think about trust mechanics when ordering from Amazon.

climax.text: Al Roth calls this 'market design': building the rules that make safe exchange possible at massive scale.

punchline.text: Great platforms make trust feel effortless.

quiz.question: What is escrow's role in platform trust?
options: It holds funds until both sides fulfill obligations

hook.text: Your credit score decides if you get a house. An algorithm you've never seen controls your financial life.

buildup.text: Increasingly, algorithms decide who to trust: credit scores, hiring filters, insurance risk models, ad targeting.

discovery.text: These systems process millions of signals humans can't, detecting fraud patterns and default risks in real time.

twist.text: But algorithmic bias is real. ZIP codes correlate with race. Past data encodes past discrimination.

climax.text: The EU's AI Act now requires explanations for high-stakes algorithmic decisions. Transparency rebuilds trust.

punchline.text: Trust the algorithm? First, audit it.

quiz.question: What is a key risk of algorithmic trust systems?

hook.text: A self-driving car must choose: swerve into a wall or hit a pedestrian. Do you trust the AI's judgment?

buildup.text: AI trust has layers: does the AI work correctly, does it act ethically, and can we verify its reasoning?

discovery.text: Research shows people overtrust AI when it's framed as 'intelligent' and undertrust it after a single visible error.

twist.text: The 'algorithm aversion' paradox: people reject algorithms that outperform humans after seeing them make one mistake.

climax.text: Building trustworthy AI requires transparency, auditing, and allowing human override—trust by design, not by faith.

punchline.text: AI earns trust the hard way: one decision at a time.

quiz.question: What is algorithm aversion?
options: Rejecting algorithms after one error despite overall superiority

hook.text: In September 2008, banks stopped lending to each other overnight. Trust vanished and the global economy froze.

buildup.text: Financial markets run on trust: banks trust banks, investors trust ratings, depositors trust banks won't fail.

discovery.text: Lehman Brothers' collapse shattered trust chains. Nobody knew who held toxic assets, so nobody would lend.

twist.text: The Fed became 'lender of last resort'—replacing collapsed private trust with government-backed trust.

climax.text: Trust collapses are nonlinear: they happen slowly, then suddenly. Recovery takes years of demonstrated reliability.

punchline.text: Markets don't crash on bad news—they crash on lost trust.

quiz.question: What caused the 2008 credit freeze?
options: Banks stopped trusting each other's solvency

hook.text: Losing $100 to a scammer hurts more than losing $100 to bad luck—even though the loss is identical.

buildup.text: Betrayal aversion means people feel extra pain when losses result from someone breaking trust intentionally.

discovery.text: Experiments show people pay more to avoid human betrayal than random loss—even when probabilities are the same.

twist.text: This makes people over-cautious after betrayal: they avoid cooperation entirely, even with trustworthy partners.

climax.text: Betrayal aversion explains why scandals devastate brands. The VW emissions fraud cost far more than the fine.

punchline.text: Betrayal scars deeper than bad luck.

quiz.question: Why does betrayal hurt more than equivalent random loss?
options: Humans feel extra pain from intentional trust violations

hook.text: A neighbor doesn't return your greeting. You stop greeting them. They think you're rude. The hostility grows.

buildup.text: Distrust spirals are self-fulfilling prophecies: suspicion breeds defensive behavior that confirms the suspicion.

discovery.text: Game theory models this as correlated defection: one defection triggers a cascade of retaliatory defections.

twist.text: The Cold War arms race was a distrust spiral: each side armed 'defensively,' each saw the other as aggressive.

climax.text: Breaking spirals needs costly, unilateral trust signals: Sadat visiting Israel in 1977 shocked the world into peace.

punchline.text: Distrust creates what it fears.

quiz.question: How can distrust spirals be broken?

hook.text: After South Africa's apartheid ended, the nation built a Truth and Reconciliation Commission instead of courts.

buildup.text: Rebuilding trust requires more than stopping harm. It demands acknowledgment, accountability, and visible change.

discovery.text: Research shows trust repairs fastest with a sequence: apology, explanation, penance, then consistent good behavior.

twist.text: But some betrayals are too deep. Studies show competence failures are forgiven faster than integrity failures.

climax.text: Germany rebuilt trust after WWII through decades of reparations, education reform, and consistent democracy.

punchline.text: Trust breaks in a moment, rebuilds over years.

quiz.question: Which type of failure is harder to recover from?

hook.text: High-trust societies are richer, healthier, and happier. But building trust requires vulnerability—risking betrayal.

buildup.text: The paradox: trust requires risk, but the reward of trust only comes after you've taken that risk.

discovery.text: Scandinavian countries top trust rankings. They also have strong safety nets that reduce the cost of betrayal.

twist.text: Low-trust societies stay trapped: nobody trusts first, so nobody cooperates, so trust never develops.

climax.text: Breaking the trap requires institutions that reduce risk: insurance, courts, guarantees that make trusting safer.

punchline.text: Trust is a leap that builds the bridge.

quiz.question: Why are high-trust societies wealthier?
options: Trust reduces transaction costs and enables cooperation
